story_text.value:
Hi HN, this is Max, Marc and Clemens, co-founders of Langfuse, the open source tool for agent & observability & evals (https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse).

It’s been a minute since our last Show HN in August 2023 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37310070) - we’ve been busy building out and serving our tracing & eval pieces over the past years and have been very lucky to build a successful company and open source project around it. Today, we are happy to show the beta of Langfuse AI Gateway: https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/tree/main/ai-gateway. You may ask, why an AI Gateway as our second product: it’s been one our community’s strongest asks + integration pattern that we’ve seen. We want to offer a scalable, reliable and secure way to solve for the gateway use case in the same way that we’ve done with tracing/evals over the past years. And we’ve recently grown our team with some excellent folks - expect to see more bigger bets from us.

Our observability SDKs currently see the code you instrument. Much of a company's model traffic runs through code that is not or cannot be easily instrumented: coding agents like Pi, Claude Code and Codex, internal tools, scripts etc. Third party gateways are already popular ways to emit traces to Langfuse and we’re happy to now ship one natively.

You change your base URL and your API key. Langfuse AI Gateway forwards the native request with a provider key that does not need to be distributed across the team. Right now, it doesn't translate between APIs, responses are relayed unchanged. This was a conscious decision to ensure stability for gateway users, as translation between e.g. OpenAI responses and Anthropic messages are imperfect and might lead to subtle failures in your agents.

If you pass a traceparent header, the call lands inside your existing Langfuse traces.

You can try by docker composing langfuse up and then on to http://localhost:3000

--

git clone https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse.git

cd langfuse

docker compose up

--

On Cloud, each call becomes a Langfuse generation with tokens, cost, latency and time to first token. Prompts and outputs are recorded if you opt in. If you self-hosted you can also track nothing, not even metadata.

Some details:

- Written in Rust. Stateless, with no database; it talks only to the Langfuse platform and the providers.

- 22MB Docker image. Under 3ms median overhead with tracing on, 1,000+ concurrent streams on 2 vCPUs.

- MIT licensed. Self-host it with Docker Compose or Helm or use our Cloud version.

- Your provider keys and contracts. We don't resell tokens.

What’s next? - Budget caps per key, user, team

- Custom model aliases and fallbacks

- Guardrails

- PII redaction

- SCIM user provisioning

We’ll be around & looking forward to all questions & comments

title.value: Show HN: Langfuse AI Gateway, open source rust gateway to trace every LLM call

story_text.value:
Hello HN!

I've spent the last few months building solutions for friends and small businesses and creating mobile applications using Claude Code and Codex. Didn't get as much traction as I would have hoped for.

Last week I spent a bit more time on running models locally on my iPhone. I wanted to see what you can get done on a model with < 4B parameters and also keep my conversation private. My initial stab at it is JackAI.

It is an AI assistant leveraging local models. It supports Apple Foundation models as well as open-weight models like Qwen 3.5 2B, Gemma 4 E2B, Whisper, etc. You can use it to chat with files, live transcription, live translation, OCR, text summarization and even deterministic actions like generating a QR code.

It is available for free in the Apple App store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/jackai-offline-ai-assistant/id...

If you have a few minutes to download it and try it out, it would be appreciated. I'm looking for feedback and impressions.

Let me know what you think!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Vera, co-founder of Wonderchat.

We started as an AI website agent that answers customer questions from a company’s website and docs. Over time, customers kept asking for the rest of the support stack around it, so we built a helpdesk: live chat, a unified inbox for email and SMS, and a help center (coming soon in a couple of weeks).

The pricing and AI native helpdesk experience is the part I most wanted to change. Most helpdesks charge per seat, so every new teammate adds to the bill, and support teams end up rationing logins. We charge one flat price with unlimited seats. You pay only for AI work: the replies and resolutions the agent handles. Human agents replying to tickets don’t cost anything extra.

We've also rebuilt the entire customer service helpdesk around the ideas of AI agent deflecting frontline support tickets first, and having an AI helpdesk agent that helps to draft auto replies to incoming tickets. As the human agent approves its responses and sends them out, the AI helpdesk agent learns about the internal support SOPs to then continually draft better AI responses.

The product is built for users to self-serve their customer service operations set up.

You don’t have to open our dashboard to set it up. Open your site’s code in Claude Code, Cursor or any coding agent and paste:

“Follow https://app.wonderchat.io/llms.txt to add a Wonderchat AI support agent to this site. Train it on [your website], test it with a few real customer questions, and add the chat widget to the shared layout.”

A few technical details:

AI answers come from our own retrieval engine, built for large and messy knowledge bases (we have customers with 10,000+ documents)

You can pick which AI model the agent runs on, so you aren’t locked into one provider

It’s still early. Helpcenter is still a build in progress. You can try it free at https://wonderchat.io/, no credit card needed.

I’d especially like feedback on the product, pricing model, and from anyone who is considering a customer service agent and ticketing software, what made you decide on Zendesk/Intercom? What would make you do the switch?

title.value: Show HN: Wonderchat – A Zendesk alternative that doesn't charge per seat

story_text.value:
Hey HN! I'm Lakshay. Raveen and I have built Cerulion, a ROS2-compatible robotics runtime written in Rust. We've worked hard on lowering IPC transport latencies without making the single process tradeoff or forcing POD message types. These fast multi-process graphs can then be resimmed deterministically, and existing ROS2 nodes/launch files can run unmodified alongside native Cerulion Rust/Python code. Installation and quickstart (with a one-shot prompt for your favorite coding agent) here at the repo README: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion

I worked on off-road autonomy during my PhD at MIT, and we kept running into inter-process latency in ROS (2 lidars and 6 cameras). Loaned messages need POD types, which nukes standard, vendor-agnostic Image/PointCloud2. We ended up running some hot paths in a brittle single process, which made debugging a nightmare. I'm sure you've seen the heisenbugs ROS-based stacks can produce, with no way to easily reproduce the consumption order or interleaving of callbacks. Valuable data of runtime failures on the robot was hard to use effectively without deterministic reproducibility.

This is what we fix. Cerulion bags record per-input reads and scheduler traces alongside message content in standard MCAPs. cerulion bag play --resim all --verify re-executes node code on the recorded schedule and compares each byte for exact matches or within defined tolerances. Exit 0 is a match, 1 shows the first topic/frame that diverges, 6 shows schedule divergence and --report gives an optional CI verdict. Eligible ROS2 processes can replay deterministically as well.

Here's the data loop:

1. Run: Dependency-ordered level-based DAG scheduler with periodic/data/sync triggers, I/O deadlines, backpressure, and automatic profiling for process partitioning. Each node by default free-runs in its own process while preserving deterministic replay. Live runs pause/resume, and UMWAIT/WFE parks idle consumers on CPUs that support it. Wall-clock reads and runtime thread spawns in user code rejected at compile time by macros.

ROS 2 is supported with rmw_cerulion for Foxy, Humble, Jazzy and Lyrical, that lets you run ROS2 nodes/launch files unmodified in the same graph as native Cerulion nodes. LD_PRELOAD gives ROS2 code shared memory loans through std::vector/std::string. cerulion ros2 attach folds in already-running ROS2 robots, and cerulion ros2 run/launch lets you run existing ROS2 workspaces on Cerulion without any additional setup (with an optional automatic migrate suggested that rewrites C++ publish sites).

2. Move: iceoryx2 shared memory with no serialization, no payload copy and no payload-sized allocation, including for variable-length messages like sensor_msgs/Image and PointCloud2. Round trip latency for a 1MiB sensor_msgs/Image between two processes is 4.08µs p50, with a tight tail of 7.38µs p99 (under 2x p50), with recording on. This is default Cerulion, against 10.95 ms for default ROS 2 Jazzy. Cerulion's p50 and p99 stay flat from 64B to 16 MiB.

3. Capture: With this round-trip latency, there are no tradeoffs, not for process isolation and not for bagging. We can afford always-on or event-based logging. Flashback is our robot dashcam: keeps ~30s of all logs and message contents in memory and saves it automatically on process crashes, topic stalls or declared incidents/manual triggers.

4. Reach: A free account lets you pair robots and desks, letting all your devices find each other with no config, IP addresses or discovery chatter. Pubsub is authenticated and on-demand, with signed grants that the robot verifies offline. We use Iroh to hole-punch or relay over WAN, and mDNS over LAN to transmit data using QUIC. Remote topics mirror into local shared memory, and each device has a single network gateway.

5. Diagnose: cerulion doctor scans for compile/run-time issues (better than Windows Troubleshooter I promise) and suggests fixes. Hindsight is an early access MCP to let agents analyze your bags.

To get started: go to the repo, install Cerulion with the curl one-liner, and paste the prompt in Claude Code/Codex: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion#quickstart-run-reco.... Or shift your own gears, it's all in the repo that you should star!

The CLI needs a free account, which we use to make device pairing as easy as AirDrop USED to be ;) Everything runs on Linux (x86_64/ARM64), macOS and Android (JNI), with more platforms coming.

We'd love to hear your feedback! If you run ROS 2 on a real robot, point this at your stack and tell us what breaks.

Docs: https://docs.cerulion.com

Site: https://cerulion.com

title.value: Show HN: Cerulion – ROS 2-compatible robotics runtime with multi-process replay

story_text.value:
Hey y'all, I'm Nick. I wanted to share a side project I started sometime last month.

I really enjoy incremental games (like Cookie Clicker, Scritchy Scratchy, etc.) and wondered if I could get a coding agent to build a new one every day that I'd actually want to play.

So I built an incremental game development harness with Claude Code. The first games were pretty rough, but I found that adding a few architectural invariants and automated playtesting around things like pacing and progression made a surprisingly big difference. They're now pretty fun most days.

My partner and I have been playing and talking about the games each day, and after some encouragement from a teammate, I figured I'd share the experiment with the HN community.

The code is available here: https://github.com/nickdirienzo/incremendle

It's AGPL in part because it uses Strudel for music generation. I've also tried to be thoughtful about crediting the artists whose work inspires the games.

Would love to hear what you think of this silly experiment!

story_text.value:
Problem: My cofounder and I work exclusively in Claude code. However, I've no idea about the conversation he is having with his agents. The only point of contact is what gets merged in Github, which is the contract. But there are times when it would be very useful for me to understand the decisions/conversation that led him to arrive at this juncture. All this context is lost.

The current best methods I've found are 1. Team/Org/Dept level shared-context.md in a cloud folder - who updates?, when?, how often?, what level of summarization?, are all unknown 2. External Tools to store context - pg, supabase, any vectordb, but then you have to maintain it, and all the same questions apply 3. Use git to share context

I've not found a single satisfactory way to achieve this. We both have multiple Claude code sessions open right now and we have no good way to communicate what each of us is trying to achieve in the session.

title.value: Ask HN: What do you all use to share context with team mates?

story_text.value:
I usually have 10+ terminals open now: a few coding agents (Claude Code, Codex), a dev server, logs, an SSH session to prod. Tabs stopped working for me (every title truncated to three letters), and tiling gets unusable past six or so panes.

Infinity Terminal is a grid that's always two rows tall and as many columns wide as you want. Every pane stays full size; you swipe sideways to reach it, or use ⌃⇥ and ⌥⌘ + arrows. There's a minimap, panes can be named and color-tinted (I keep prod red), SSH sessions get a stable color per host, any pane can expand to the full column, and the whole layout comes back after a restart.

A few details for people running agents: drag-select works inside Claude Code even though it captures the mouse, ⌥⌘C copies a command that Claude Code hard-wrapped back as one line, and microphone access works for /voice.

It's Swift/AppKit on SwiftTerm, signed and notarized, MIT. The first version was Electron; this is a full native rewrite. Site with an interactive demo: https://infinityterminal.com · Homebrew: brew install --cask bujna94/tap/infinity-terminal

Happy to hear what breaks.

title.value: Show HN: Infinity Terminal – a native macOS terminal with endless columns

It's Swift/AppKit on SwiftTerm, signed and notarized, MIT. The first version was Electron; this is a full native rewrite. Site with an interactive demo: https://infinityterminal.com · Homebrew: brew install --cask bujna94/tap/infinity-terminal

Happy to hear what breaks.

story_text.value:
Hello, HN! I’m Max, CTO at Hystax. We use Claude a lot in our development work, and we’re also trying to make coding agents cheaper to run. We built the open-source Kompressor for compressing identical tool outputs that agents constantly resend. In our Codex tests, we noticed a real cost reduction of 22.7%. But testing it with Claude Code, we found something completely different. In Claude Code, the cache plays a more crucial role than compression.

Claude Code marks its messages with caching points. As a result, almost every request consists of a long cached prefix and a new, truncated final part. Based on practical experience with Opus 5.5, reading from the cache appears to cost $0.20 per million tokens, accounting for about 92–95% of the tokens charged for prompts. Meanwhile, a five-minute cache entry costs $5, which is 25 times more expensive than reading from the cache. When an agent needs to run a build or a longer training cycle, they face the problem of the cache expiring. The next request then has to write the prefix to the cache again. We saw this 33 times in a cycle of 89-task runs without compression. As a result, 927,000 tokens were rewritten, which is approximately one-third of the volume billed in full.

Until now, we’ve deliberately left the Claude Code text uncompressed because overwriting any byte within a cached prefix would very likely cause it to become invalid. But here’s what we came up with instead:

– Compress only the uncached part. On the first transmission, only the new part is compressed. Everything already cached stays byte-for-byte unchanged. Fragments shorter than 4,000 characters are sent in full, since compressing each fragment would be much more expensive than sending the entire dialogue as is.

– Keep the cache active while the tools are running; don’t let it expire. While the agent waits for a tool response (model building/training), Kompressor resends the last request every 4.5 minutes with max_tokens: 1, so Anthropic re-reads the cached dialogue, and the five-minute timer restarts. Pings stop on the agent’s next request, after ~50 min, on the first failed attempt, or if a ping finds nothing in the cache.

– Switch to the one-hour cache only when necessary. After the first pause longer than 5 min, Kompressor requests a one-hour cache for that conversation.

We ran Claude Code on the Opus 5.5 model through the Terminal-Bench 2.1 benchmark (89 tasks) and calculated the cost based on Anthropic's actual billing, including pings. The cost per run decreased from $35.35 to $28.30 (-20%). The percentage of tasks solved by the agent without compression was 89.9%, and 90.6% when using Kompressor. The number of tokens lost due to cache expiration decreased from 927,000 to 13,000.

But there’s a caveat: the agent never solves the same task twice in exactly the same way, and the entire difference came down to just 4 out of the 89 tasks. We expect these savings to persist from run to run: about 11% from keeping the cache up to date, and a few more percentage points from compression. This effect is most noticeable on tasks where the agent waits a long time – more than five minutes – for a command to execute: model training, compilation, and long simulations. In those cases, costs decreased by 34%. To try Kompressor, see the GitHub repo below. Setup is in the README. The default configuration already includes compression of new text only and a switch to an hourly cache on long pauses; “keep-warm” is off (the only request that the proxy sends on its own). To enable, add to your config:

     [proxy.providers.anthropic] 
     cache_keep_warm = true
and then run:

    kompressor wrap claude 
>
The benchmark above was run with all these settings enabled.

Here are cost calculations: https://optscale.ai/blog/claude-code-prompt-caching If you run long tasks in Claude Code, how often does the cache expire while a tool is still running? Have you seen this with other providers too?

story_text.value:
Hey hn, i'm Armel solo dev from Abidjan. I built upstar a github trending like website where projects are ranked by how fast they grow in each topic

I love discovering new projects, so I spend a lot of my time scrolling Reddit and X. I thought, why not get the trending projects I care about in my inbox, like I already get good articles from Medium? I looked at GitHub Trending, but it mostly shows big projects. It's hard to find small projects that also deserve attention. So I built this tool.

There are 69 topics, from programming languages to subjects like agent skills, reverse engineering, emulation, etc. The score is the stars gained in the current period (day, week or month) divided by the square root of the stars the project had before that period. So small projects can rank above big projects, even if the big ones gain more stars.

I try my best to keep malicious projects out without penalizing good small legit projects. Each project is analyzed by judges (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus) that follow rules I set. Two weeks ago I reported a malware campaign of 479 repos to GitHub, and most of the accounts behind it are gone now. This week I found 333 more that sent people to installers outside GitHub.

You can browse the site freely, with no ads and no tracking. To get the Monday digest for the topics you choose, you sign in with GitHub, or just leave your email. There's also an MCP server, for people who prefer to ask their AI agent directly.

I built the project with the help of Claude Code, and the short repo summaries are written by AI. The hardest part was putting projects in the right topics. That's why I'd love your feedback on the rankings and the topics, if any of this speaks to you.
